phrases: In June, twenty twenty-three, a submersible diving to the Titanic was crushed inward, in a few milliseconds.
Five people were on board.
None of them survived.
This is how the deep sea's pressure works, why the Titan's hull was so unusual, and what changed afterwards.
The Titanic lies about three thousand eight hundred metres down, at the bottom of the North Atlantic.
Every ten metres of seawater adds about one more atmosphere of pressure.
So down there, it's around three hundred and eighty times the pressure at the surface.
That's almost four hundred kilograms pressing on every square centimetre.
Like a grand piano, balanced on your fingertip.
Anything hollow down there is being squeezed from every direction at once.
Send an empty soda can down there, and it wouldn't just dent.
It would be crushed flat, long before it reached the bottom.
Most deep-diving submersibles carry their crew inside a sphere of thick titanium or steel.
A sphere is the ideal shape.
The pressure pushes evenly over the whole surface, so no spot carries more than its share.
The research sub Alvin has made more than five thousand dives like this, with its crew inside a titanium sphere.
And engineers have decades of tests showing exactly how those metals behave, dive after dive.
Titan was different.
Its middle was a tube of carbon fibre, about thirteen centimetres thick, built up from layers of fibre and glue.
At each end, a titanium dome, joined to the tube by titanium rings, glued in place.
A tube holds more people than a sphere.
And carbon fibre is light, and incredibly strong when you pull on it.
But deep underwater, a hull isn't pulled. It's squeezed.
And for thick carbon fibre under squeezing, again and again, there's far less proof.
Its layers can start to separate, and the damage hides inside.
And carbon fibre and titanium squeeze by different amounts, which loads the joints between them.
It was a new kind of hull, taking people this deep, and it was never certified by an outside inspector.
Every dive loads the hull with that enormous pressure, and every ascent releases it.
Each cycle can grow tiny damage.
A gap between layers.
A weak spot in the glue.
Titan had sensors to listen for cracking, meant to warn the pilot in time to head back up.
But a warning only helps if there's time to act, and if someone decides to stop.
On a dive in twenty twenty-two, the people aboard heard a loud bang.
Investigators later concluded the hull was most likely damaged around then.
It kept diving.
On the eighteenth of June, twenty twenty-three, Titan began its dive toward the Titanic.

An implosion like that is over in a few milliseconds.
Far faster than anyone on board could have noticed.
For four days, the world searched.

The company that built Titan suspended all its operations soon after the accident.
Certified deep submersibles are inspected by outside experts, and their hulls are pressure-tested beyond the depth they'll dive to.
